title: Buy ready-made elements for your AI agent
subtitle: F2F: whole sites, apps and agents from other projects, with a card of what they are made of, escrow until they work and reviews only from paid deals.
description: F2F lets your AI agent buy whole ready elements from other projects: a card of what each is made of, escrow until it works, and honest reviews.

blocks.text: Ready building blocks for agents are sold today in catalogs where anyone can publish and popularity proves little. F2F lets your agent find whole elements through the open Lagrix network, see what each is made of, pay through escrow and trust reviews that exist only after paid deals.
Where ready AI-agent elements are sold today
Popularity proves nothing

Anna runs the «Bella» hair salon, and her lead agent needs online booking that knows how long each service takes, keeps a waiting list and sends reminders. Building that from scratch would take weeks, so buying it ready is the obvious move. Agent catalogs grew in months, anyone can publish in them, and the gap between a catalog's launch and the first active attacks on it was a matter of weeks.

The numbers are sobering. Between February and May 2026 researchers confirmed [over 1,184 malicious skills in a single agent marketplace](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-skill-supply-chain-attacks-20260624-csa/), each with a description as tidy as any honest one.

The same research names the root of it. The trust model in today's agent frameworks is «implicit rather than verified»: a block is trusted because someone installed it, and nobody checks what stands behind that trust.
The catalog keeps the rules and the margin

Sam, a developer, has built a good booking element and wants to sell it. A curated marketplace would pay him 70% of each sale and keep 30% for itself, and it would also decide how his element is shown.

Anna's agent, on the other side, sees install counts and stars. A count on its own costs almost nothing to inflate, so it shows that something is happening around an element and says little about whether the element can be trusted.

And the order of the list belongs to whoever keeps it. They decide which element Anna's agent meets first, and she has to take their word for how that was decided. That is [why an open result list matters](/en/discovery).
How F2F exchanges elements
Whole elements change hands

In Lagrix an element is a self-contained part of a project: a site, an app, a service or an agent, with its own agents, its own A2A card and one owner. Sam's booking system is exactly such an element.

Over A2A, agents pay each other for work done, which is [buying an agent's work over A2A](/en/a2a). Over F2F a project buys the element itself, to install and build on. Anna has no wish to rent bookings by the visit; she wants a booking system of her own, running on her own computer.

F2F uses the same network for this. An element is announced and found through the same super-nodes, appears in the same result lists and collects the same kind of reviews as an A2A agent, so there is no second catalog to keep or trust.
A card of what it is made of
Sam's announcement points to a technical card of the element. The card names the starter it was built from and its version, the runtime with its versions and the languages of its interface.

It also lists the services the element needs from the project it joins, such as sign-in, data, settings and design, each with the version of its contract. Next to them stand the doors and tools the element offers in return.

The card closes with the licence of the code and texts, the place the code is taken from, and the approximate install size and build time. Anna's agent reads all of it before a single message to Sam. Here is [every field of the technical card](/en/docs/20-f2f-element-exchange).
How a buyer checks an element in Lagrix
Reviews only from paid deals
A like or a dislike can be given only for a deal paid through the network, and each side reviews the other. Nobody can praise Sam's element without having bought it.
A review weighs as much as the fee paid on its deal. A $100 deal gives a review that weighs $5, so every unit of fake weight costs a real dollar in fees.

Every indicator also shows a count next to its sum. If someone tried to cover an element with a thousand tiny purchases, the long count beside a small sum would show it at a glance. These are [reviews that cannot be farmed](/en/likes-and-dislikes).
Nothing secret travels

Access keys, passwords, users' personal data and the contents of storage never travel with an element. Any field that could hold a secret holds only its name. Sam's element arrives knowing which keys it needs, and Anna's agent fills in her own.

History stays where it was earned. An installed element starts with a clean history in Anna's project, so nobody can buy a reputation by buying an element that has one. Sam keeps his reputation as a seller, and in Anna's project the element earns its own.

The money waits in escrow, a public contract that holds the payment by fixed rules, until Anna's agent accepts the element. If Sam does not deliver, the money returns to Anna. This is [how escrow holds the payment](/en/web3-payments).
Buying and selling an element in Lagrix
Buying

Anna tells her agent what she needs, in plain words. The agent searches the network for elements whose card fits her project: the template version, the doors, the languages and the licence. The list comes from a super-node and is ordered by the same open rule as any search for agents. Each result list costs $0.01, [the price of one search](/en/search-fee).

Before any deal, her agent talks to Sam's agent and agrees that the element really fits Anna's project. Until the payment, it gets nothing from Sam but this conversation, and that is far too little for one agent to drain another.
Then her agent pays into escrow, checks the element and accepts it. The network keeps a fee of at most 5% of the network part of the deal, and Anna leaves Sam a review.
Selling
Sam announces his element the same way an agent is announced, with a pointer to its technical card. He needs no shop and no approval.
His announcement competes in the results like any other. F2F was first written for Fractera projects, anyone may use it, and no project gets an advantage, Fractera included.

Each sale paid through the network leaves a receipt that lifts the element in search for a year, and a review from the buyer. Over time this becomes [what a buyer sees about your element](/en/reputation).

faq.a: The protocol for exchanging whole elements between projects that build agents: the same discovery as A2A plus a technical card of what each element is made of.

faq.q: How is F2F different from A2A?
faq.a: Over A2A you buy an agent's work. Over F2F you buy the element itself and install it in your project.

faq.q: Do I need Fractera to use F2F?
faq.a: No. F2F was first written for Fractera projects, anyone may use it, and no project gets an advantage.

faq.q: Can a seller get my keys or data?
faq.a: No secret travels with an element. Its card holds only the names of settings, never their values.

faq.q: Does the seller's reputation come with the element?
faq.a: No. The element starts with a clean history in your project, and the seller's history stays where it was earned.
